321 I kept on wandering, until the gods loosed me from my afflictions;
322 till on that day in the rich-settled land of the Phaeacian people
323 you gave me courage in speech and yourself led me to the city.
324 Now by your father I clasp your knees—for I do not imagine
325 that I have come to clear-seen Ithaca, no, but some other
326 land I am roaming in; and I think you are only in mockery
327 saying these things, so that you may beguile and bewilder my spirit—
328 tell me if truly indeed I have reached my beloved home-country.”
329 Then in answer to him spoke the goddess gray-eyed Athena:
330 “Always this sort of a mind is there inside of your bosom;
331 therefore I cannot abandon you there in your pain and your sorrow,
332 since you are gentle and keen of wit and steady in judgment.
333 Any other man, coming home from his wanderings, would be eager
334 straightway within his halls to behold his children and consort;
335 but to you it is not yet dear to be told or be certain,
336 not till you make trial still of your wife, who in equal constancy
337 sits there within your halls, and for her in continual sorrow
338 nights and days waste away as she sheds her tears without ceasing.
339 Yet for my part I never at all was doubtful, but in my spirit
340 knew you would come home again, though bereft of all your companions;
341 but I was not willing to fight with Poseidon against you,
342 my father's brother, who stored up wrath in the depth of his spirit,
343 angered because you had blinded the eye of the son he beloved.
344 But come, I will show you the seat of Ithaca, that you may trust me.
345 This is the harbor of Phorcys, the old man lord of the seaward;
346 and here at the head of the harbor stands the long-leafed olive;
347 and close beside it a lovely cave wrapped over in dimness,
348 sacred to nymphs, the ones that are called by men the Naiads.
349 This is the arching cavern where many and many a great gift
350 you used to perform for the nymphs, full-finished hecatombs there;
351 and this is Neriton mountain, clothed all over with forest.”
352 So the goddess spoke, and scattered the mist, and the country appeared clear.
353 Then did the great-enduring noble Odysseus feel gladness,
354 rejoicing in his own land, and he kissed the grain-giving earth there.
355 Straightway he prayed to the nymphs, lifting his hands up before them:
356 “Naiad nymphs, daughters of Zeus, I had never expected
357 ever to see you again; but now with gentle entreaties
358 hail, and we will give gifts, as we did in the time that is bygone,
359 if the daughter of Zeus, who drives the spoil, in her kindness will grant me
360 life for myself, and bring my beloved son on into manhood.”
361 Then to him once more spoke the goddess gray-eyed Athena:
362 “Take heart; do not let these matters trouble your mind any longer.
363 Rather, let us at once in the inmost part of the wondrous
364 cave put away these possessions, so all may remain safe for you there;
365 then let us both take counsel how everything best may be managed.”
366 So the goddess spoke, and entered the cave wrapped over in dimness,
367 seeking the hiding-places throughout the cavern; and then Odysseus
368 carried all inward close by, the gold and the tireless bronze there,
369 and the well-fashioned garments the Phaeacians had given him.
370 All these he carefully stored, and over the doorway a great stone
371 Pallas Athena set fast, the daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus.
372 Then the two of them sat by the foot of the sacred olive tree there
373 and were devising destruction for all the arrogant suitors.
374 First among them in speech began the goddess gray-eyed Athena:
375 “Son of Laertes, seed of Zeus, Odysseus of many devices,
376 plan how you shall lay hands on the shameless troop of the suitors,
377 who now for three full years have been lording it over your household,
378 courting your godlike wife and presenting the gifts of their wooing.
379 Yet she, with longing always in heart for your homeward returning,
380 gives hope to every man and promises each one in turn there,
381 sending messages forth, while the mind in her longs for another.”
382 Then in answer to her spoke Odysseus of many devices:
383 “Ah me, then surely I too like Agamemnon son of Atreus
384 should have met a disastrous doom in the midst of my halls and my household,
385 if you, goddess, had not recounted each thing in its due order.
386 Come then, weave me a stratagem, how I shall punish them for it;
387 and you yourself stand near me, and breathe bold force into my spirit,
388 as in the day when we loosed the shining frontlet of Troia.
389 If with such eagerness you would stand there beside me, gray-eyed one,
390 then with you I could fight against even three hundred fighters,
391 with you, revered goddess, if with ready heart you would aid me.”
392 Then in answer to him spoke the goddess gray-eyed Athena:
393 “Surely I will be beside you, and you will not fail to perceive me,
394 when the time comes that we must be busy about these endeavors;
395 and I think many a man of the suitors who raven your livelihood
396 will befoul the broad floor with blood and with brains all together.
397 But come, I will make you unknown to the sight of all mortals.
398 I will shrivel the beautiful flesh on the limbs of your supple body,
399 strip from your head the bright hair, and around you cast a poor garment
400 such that a man would abhor to behold it upon any wearer.
